subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: After acetylcholine has acted on the postsynaptic membrane, it is broken down by acetylcholinesterase. The importance of this is to:
options: Prevent continuous stimulation so the synapse can respond to new impulses
Increase the size of the next action potential
Provide energy for the next impulse
questions.explain: Hydrolysing acetylcholine stops prolonged depolarisation, allowing the receptors to reset and the products to be recycled.

questions.q: How many molecules of ATP and reduced NADP are used to convert two molecules of GP into two molecules of TP in one turn of the Calvin cycle?
questions.explain: Reducing two GP to two TP requires two ATP and two reduced NADP per turn of the cycle.

questions.q: Besides reduced NAD, what TWO products result from the link reaction per pyruvate molecule?
options: Acetyl coenzyme A and carbon dioxide
questions.explain: Each pyruvate is decarboxylated and combined with coenzyme A to form acetyl CoA, releasing CO2 and reducing NAD.

questions.q: In glycolysis, the six-carbon hexose bisphosphate is split to form two molecules of which three-carbon compound?
questions.explain: Hexose bisphosphate is lysed into two molecules of triose phosphate, each of which is then oxidised to pyruvate.

questions.q: What is the approximate respiratory quotient (RQ) for the complete aerobic respiration of a carbohydrate such as glucose?
questions.explain: For glucose the volumes of CO2 produced and O2 consumed are equal, giving an RQ of 1.0.

questions.q: The basement membrane of the glomerulus prevents which component of blood from entering the filtrate?
questions.explain: The basement membrane acts as a molecular sieve, holding back large plasma proteins and blood cells while small molecules pass through.

questions.q: In mammalian muscle during anaerobic respiration, what is the key role of reducing pyruvate to lactate?
options: To produce carbon dioxide for gas exchange
To regenerate NAD so glycolysis can continue
To synthesise acetyl CoA for the Krebs cycle
questions.explain: Reducing pyruvate oxidises reduced NAD back to NAD, allowing glycolysis and its ATP yield to continue without oxygen.

questions.q: Why does reduced FAD ultimately lead to the synthesis of fewer ATP molecules than reduced NAD?
options: FAD is produced only in the cytoplasm
FAD donates its electrons at a later point on the chain, pumping fewer protons
FAD carries no electrons, only protons
FAD is not used by the electron transport chain
questions.explain: FAD feeds electrons in further along the chain than NAD, so fewer protons are pumped and less ATP is made.

questions.q: In a relaxed muscle, the myosin-binding sites on actin are blocked by:
options: Tropomyosin held in place by troponin
questions.explain: At rest, tropomyosin covers the binding sites on actin, with troponin holding it there until calcium ions arrive.

questions.q: How does cyclic photophosphorylation differ from non-cyclic photophosphorylation?
options: It occurs in the stroma and fixes carbon dioxide
It uses photosystem II only and reduces NADP
It produces oxygen but no ATP
It involves only photosystem I and produces ATP but no reduced NADP
questions.explain: In cyclic flow, electrons from photosystem I return to it, generating ATP without photolysis or reduced NADP.

questions.q: In which cellular location does glycolysis occur, and which type of phosphorylation produces its ATP?
questions.explain: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm and generates ATP directly by substrate-level phosphorylation.

questions.q: Phosphocreatine is important in muscle contraction because it:
options: Provides the calcium needed for contraction
Rapidly regenerates ATP from ADP at the start of intense exercise
questions.explain: Phosphocreatine donates a phosphate to ADP to quickly resynthesise ATP, sustaining contraction during short bursts of activity.

questions.q: How many turns of the Calvin cycle are needed to produce one molecule of glucose?
questions.explain: Each turn fixes one CO2 and produces one usable triose phosphate; six turns provide the six carbons of one glucose.

questions.q: How is ATP generated during the light-dependent reactions?
options: By substrate-level phosphorylation in the stroma
By the direct action of light on ADP
By chemiosmosis as protons flow through ATP synthase in the thylakoid membrane
questions.explain: Protons accumulate in the thylakoid space and flow back through ATP synthase, driving photophosphorylation by chemiosmosis.

questions.q: In the second messenger model of glucagon action, the binding of glucagon to its receptor leads to:
options: Activation of adenylate cyclase, raising cyclic AMP, which activates protein kinase A
Direct entry of glucagon into the cell to activate enzymes
questions.explain: Glucagon activates adenylate cyclase, producing cAMP as a second messenger that activates protein kinase A to trigger glycogenolysis.

questions.q: In non-cyclic photophosphorylation, what happens to an electron when light strikes the reaction centre of a photosystem?
options: It is excited to a higher energy level and passed to an electron acceptor
questions.explain: Light energy excites an electron, which is then captured by an electron acceptor and passed along the electron transport chain.

questions.q: What is the immediate source of the electrons that replace those lost from photosystem II during non-cyclic photophosphorylation?
questions.explain: Photolysis splits water, supplying electrons to photosystem II as well as protons and oxygen.

questions.q: When the body overheats, heat loss is increased by:
options: Vasodilation of skin arterioles and increased sweating
questions.explain: Vasodilation brings more warm blood to the skin surface and sweating removes heat by evaporation, both increasing heat loss.

questions.q: ADH is produced by the hypothalamus and released from the:
questions.explain: ADH is synthesised in the hypothalamus and stored in and released from the posterior pituitary gland.

questions.q: Which statement about the role of reduced NAD and reduced FAD in respiration is correct?
options: They directly phosphorylate ADP to ATP
They deliver electrons and protons to the electron transport chain
They are the final electron acceptors of the chain
They are produced only during oxidative phosphorylation
questions.explain: Reduced coenzymes carry electrons and protons to the carriers on the inner membrane, feeding the chain.

questions.q: The counter-current multiplier in the loop of Henle works because:
options: Both limbs are equally permeable to water and ions
The ascending limb is permeable to water but not ions
The descending limb actively pumps in water
The ascending limb actively pumps out sodium ions, creating a high solute concentration (low water potential) in the medulla
questions.explain: Active removal of Na+ from the impermeable-to-water ascending limb builds a medullary solute gradient that draws water out of the descending limb and collecting duct.

questions.q: Apart from photolysis, what is the other source of protons that builds up inside the thylakoid space?
options: Protons carried across the membrane by electron carriers
questions.explain: As electrons pass along the thylakoid electron carriers, protons are pumped from the stroma into the thylakoid space.

questions.q: Which molecule is phosphorylated using ATP at the start of glycolysis, before the sugar is split?
questions.explain: Glucose is first phosphorylated to glucose phosphate, making it more reactive before it is split into two triose phosphates.

questions.q: In the eye, the iris controls the amount of light reaching the retina. In bright light, the:
options: Pupil dilates to admit more light
Radial muscles contract to widen the pupil
Circular muscles contract to constrict the pupil
questions.explain: Bright light triggers a reflex in which the circular muscles of the iris contract, narrowing the pupil to protect the retina.

questions.q: Why does anaerobic respiration yield far less ATP per glucose than aerobic respiration?
options: Lactate stores most of the energy as ATP
Only substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis occurs; the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation do not
More ATP is invested at the start
questions.explain: Without oxygen, only the small net ATP yield of glycolysis is obtained, as the oxygen-dependent stages cannot proceed.

questions.q: What overall role does the chloroplast envelope (double membrane) play?
options: It is the site of the Calvin cycle
It controls the entry and exit of substances such as CO2 and sugars
questions.explain: The chloroplast envelope regulates exchange of materials, including the movement of CO2 in and products out.

questions.q: A desert mammal that produces very concentrated urine is likely to have:
options: A glomerulus that filters very little blood
A long loop of Henle, allowing a steep medullary solute gradient
A very short loop of Henle
questions.explain: A long loop of Henle generates a stronger medullary concentration gradient, enabling more water reabsorption and highly concentrated urine.

questions.q: Depolarisation during an action potential is caused by:
options: Potassium ions diffusing out of the axon
Voltage-gated sodium channels opening and Na+ flooding into the axon
questions.explain: At threshold, voltage-gated Na+ channels open and Na+ rushes in, making the inside positive (depolarisation).

questions.q: In which direction are protons pumped to create the gradient that drives ATP synthesis in the chloroplast?
options: From the stroma into the thylakoid space
From the cytoplasm into the stroma
From the thylakoid space into the stroma
questions.explain: Protons are moved into the thylakoid space, and their return to the stroma through ATP synthase generates ATP.

questions.q: When CO2 is fixed onto the 5-carbon RuBP, what is the immediate product?
questions.explain: The unstable 6-carbon intermediate splits at once into two 3-carbon molecules of GP.
